newsitem.title: UK: Mark hammered by EMU, Greenspan and trend-lovers.
newsitem.headline: Mark hammered by EMU, Greenspan and trend-lovers.

text.p: The mark sank further on its European cross rates Wednesday, spiralling lower against free floating currencies which are unlikely to take part in the now almost certain launch of Europe's single currency in 1999.

The latest body blow to the mark was delivered indirectly by Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan Tuesday, however, who sent U.S. stocks, bonds and dollar/mark soaring by giving a rosy scenario of assessment of long-term U.S. inflation and growth.
Sterling/mark followed suit and exaggerated mark sales.
Yet, analysts said the big picture is still of independent mark weakness and the latest instalment of EMU optimism.
"The market is really frothing up and we're getting talk like dollar/mark at two-to-one," said Teis Knuthsen, economist at First Chicago in London.

"The story is still of mark weakness in the face of EMU, however, and the latest comments from the Bundesbank about deficits of 3.2 or 3.3 percent of GDP being acceptable show the last hurdle to a 1999 start has probably been cleared."

Analysts said the French 1997 budget projections on Monday show France does not expect to meet the 3.0 percent deficit target exactly. Comments from Germany and France since show this is unlikely to prevent monetary union starting on time.

Three senior Bundesbank officials said Tuesday that the Maastricht Treaty did not specify the 3.0 percent deficit/output ratio be met exactly but that sustainability of the deficit reductions was more important. Hans Juergen Krupp said it was unfounded that the euro would not be stable if deficit were slightly above the 3.0 percent level.

Traders said the acceptance of deviations from the 3.0 percent deficit target will make it more difficult for Germany to object to the inclusion in the single currency of currencies seen as traditionally less stable, like the Italian lira. This in itself is creating jitters about the stability of the euro.

French finance minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn, meantime, actively advocated the inclusion of Italy, Spain and Portugal in the first wave of EMU in an interview with German weekly Die Zeit. He also said convergence was more important for EMU entry than hitting an exact target.

The now very real prospect of the mark's disappearance into an uncertain euro in less than 18 months time has combined with a horizon of relatively low German interest rates and prolonged European economic restructuring to push traders out of the German unit for now and out of its likely affiliates in EMU.
The lack of central bank protests at its fall aids the move.
"This is a story of mark weakness, more so than dollar or sterling strength," said Joe Prendergast, head of currency research and strategy at CSFB.
"You only have to look at dollar/Swiss, which despite the surge in dollar/mark to new ranges, has yet to break its high for the year."

Apart from the dollar, sterling and yen, the big beneficiaries of mark sales were the Swiss franc, Swedish and Norwegian crowns -- all seen as non-EMU havens. Mark/Swiss fell to a 10-month low at 82.19 in early trade while mark/Sweden slumped to its lowest level since December 1992.

Currencies now expected to start EMU, like the French franc and Spanish peseta and Italian lira, were little changed against the mark as investors stayed cautious of the Euro zone. Concern about recent mark purchases by the Bank of Italy and Bank of Spain also kept traders wary of pesetas and lira, said analysts.

At 1030 GMT, mark/French franc was at 3.3700/05 compared with 3.3687/92 late Tuesday. Mark/lira was at 971.50/2.00 compared with 971.75/85 late yesterday. Mark/Spain was at 84.17/19 versus 84.17/18 on Tuesday.
Provisional July inflation data was released from the west German states, meantime, but had little market impact.

A higher-than-expected 0.5 percent rise in consumer prices in North-Rhine Westphalia, Hesse and Bavaria was partly attributed to the reecnt weakness of the mark but few saw the rise as raising sufficient concern at the Bundesbank to push up interest rates anytime soon.

The Bundesbank council meeting Thursday will be watched closely amid lingering talk the central bank may move to variable rate repurchase tenders, which would allow market rates to tick higher in response to further mark weakness. Most analysts contacted said this was unlikely, however.
-- Mike Dolan, London newsroom +44 1761 542 6762
